newsitem.title: USA: U.S. counters scandal charges at Taiwan institute.
newsitem.headline: U.S. counters scandal charges at Taiwan institute.

text.p: The United States dismissed as exaggerated and often "just plain wrong" allegations by the former head of Washington's de facto embassy in Taipei that staff extorted sex and money from visa applicants.
The allegations are "overstated, they are based on highly questionable evidence and often they are just plain wrong," State Department spokesman Glyn Davies told a regular news conference.

He said James Wood, whose charges swept Taiwan this weekend, had resigned under official pressure after little more than a year in his post because he "refused to accept State Department direction and oversight" and failed to establish good working relations with Taiwanese authorities.

Wood took the post based at the American Institute in Taiwan's Arlington, Virginia, headquarters outside Washington in December 1995 and left in January this year. He says he was forced out when he tried to shed light on what he called widespread corruption at AIT.
Wood was the chairman of AIT, the Washington-funded agency that handles U.S. interests in the absence of diplomatic relations.

In reports in the Taiwan media, Wood, now in Washington, alleged that institute staff took bribes, that $5.3 million in visa fees was missing and that a visa investigator forced at least one applicant to trade sex for a visa approval.
Responding to the reports, Davies said the source of much material seemed to be a Taiwan national hired by AIT in 1985 to verify information provided by prospective immigrants to the United States.
"In 1990 we terminated this individual's employment for official misconduct involving his assigned duties," he said.
He said an allegation in 1993 that individuals had paid $20,000 to $25,000 for visas was investigated by the State Department.
The investigators concluded that the allegations were baseless, "and indeed may have been made with the specific purpose of discrediting honest AIT officers," Davies said.

He said the only case of alleged sexual impropriety the department was aware of dated back to 1989, when a woman who had applied for an immigrant visa from the AIT alleged that a local employee visited her and made unwanted sexual advances.

"AIT investigated the case immediately. The employee denied the charge. That employee subsequently retired. As far as we know the woman never filed legal charges. How you get from that to the conclusion of Mr Wood's manifesto that there were thousands of people being sexually harassed is quite a leap and quite a stretch," Davies said.
He denied suggestions the State Department had covered up the incidents, saying: "I would deny the State Department has covered up any malfeasance or corruption at AIT."

On the charge over missing visa fees, Davies conceded there was "an ongoing dispute over accounting for a portion of ... visa fees at AIT." But he said: "There's no missing $5.3 million. We're talking about how they were accounted for and perhaps how they should have been accounted for."

Apart from the allegation over AIT irregularities, the U.S. Justice Department is investigating reports that Wood improperly pressured Taiwanese businessmen to contribute to President Bill Clinton's re-election campaign.
